note: A troubleshooting handbook for people with no engineering background. Default setup: STM32F103C8T6 "Blue Pill" + ST-Link V2 + PlatformIO CLI on macOS + Arduino framework (STM32duino), with a CH340 USB-to-serial adapter. Every entry follows the same shape: symptom → signals → causes ranked by likelihood (each with a check you can do in a minute, and a fix) → a plain-English explanation → a question you can paste straight into an AI. The probabilities are rules of thumb from experience, not statistics. Start with the "high" ones and rule them out one at a time. Don't change three things at once.

entries.symptom: I just installed PlatformIO, but when I type pio in the terminal it says command not found

causes.cause: pio got installed into a folder that isn't on your PATH (for example ~/.platformio/penv/bin or uv's tools folder), so the terminal doesn't know where to look
causes.check: Run ls ~/.platformio/penv/bin/pio or ls ~/.local/bin/pio and see whether the file exists
causes.fix: Add that folder to your PATH: append export PATH="$HOME/.platformio/penv/bin:$PATH" to the end of ~/.zshrc (adjust the path to match yours), then run source ~/.zshrc or open a new terminal

causes.cause: You didn't open a new terminal after installing, so the old terminal still has the old PATH
causes.check: Open a brand-new terminal window and type pio --version
causes.fix: Close every terminal window and reopen; the terminal inside VS Code needs to be reopened too

causes.cause: The install actually failed partway through and the error scrolled past unnoticed
causes.check: Scroll back through the install output looking for a red Error; or run find ~ -name pio -type f 2>/dev/null to search your whole home folder
causes.fix: Run the install again, and this time watch the output all the way to the last line

entries.explain: PATH is like the terminal's contact list: it only looks for commands in the folders on that list. If pio is installed but its folder was never added to the list, the terminal acts like it doesn't exist.
entries.ask_ai: I installed PlatformIO on macOS and typing pio gives command not found. My shell is zsh. The output of `ls ~/.platformio/penv/bin` is: [paste]. Help me add it to my PATH and tell me exactly which file to edit.

entries.symptom: Installing PlatformIO complains about my Python version, or says it can't find python at all
signals: SyntaxError: invalid syntax (inside the install script)

causes.cause: The python3 that ships with macOS is just a stub; the first time you use it, it asks you to install the Xcode Command Line Tools
causes.check: Type python3 --version in the terminal; if a dialog pops up offering to install developer tools, this is it
causes.fix: Click Install and wait for it to finish (a few minutes), or install a standalone Python 3.11+ with uv or Homebrew

causes.cause: You have several Pythons on the system and the terminal is defaulting to an old one
causes.check: Run which -a python3 to see how many there are, then run each one with --version
causes.fix: Let uv manage it: uv python install 3.11, then uv tool install platformio. That sidesteps the system Python entirely

causes.cause: You typed python instead of python3 (macOS dropped the plain python command years ago)
causes.check: Swap python for python3 in the command and try again
causes.fix: Always use python3 / pip3, or just use uv

entries.explain: PlatformIO itself is a program written in Python, so it needs a recent-enough Python as its foundation. If the foundation is missing or too old, the house won't stand.
entries.ask_ai: I'm installing PlatformIO on macOS and running into a Python problem. The output of `which -a python3` and `python3 --version` is: [paste]. The error is: [paste]. I'd like to manage Python with uv; please give me the complete steps.

entries.symptom: The install says Permission denied, or asks for an admin password that I don't want to (or can't) enter

causes.cause: It's trying to write into a system folder (/usr/bin, /Library) that a regular user isn't allowed to touch
causes.check: Look at the path in the error message: does it start with /usr or /Library?
causes.fix: Don't sudo pip. Use an install method that only writes to your home folder: uv tool install platformio, or pip3 install --user platformio

causes.cause: At some point you installed something with sudo, which made root the owner of ~/.platformio or ~/.local
causes.check: Run ls -la ~ | grep platformio and see whether the owner column says root
causes.fix: sudo chown -R $(whoami) ~/.platformio (this one step needs your password once; after that you won't need it)

causes.cause: The downloaded script isn't marked as executable
causes.check: Run ls -l on the script and see whether the permissions column has an x in it
causes.fix: chmod +x scriptname, or just run it with python3 scriptname

entries.explain: macOS keeps its system folders locked, and the key is the admin password. PlatformIO doesn't need to go anywhere near those folders. Installing it in your own home folder is all it takes.
entries.ask_ai: Installing PlatformIO on macOS gives Permission denied. Full error: [paste]. I don't want to use sudo. Please give me a way to install it only into my user folder.

entries.symptom: My first build gets stuck downloading the platform or toolchain, spins forever, then dies with a network error

causes.cause: The connection to PlatformIO's servers is slow or keeps dropping (flaky Wi-Fi, a VPN, or a proxy in the way)
causes.check: Open https://registry.platformio.org in your browser and see whether it loads instantly
causes.fix: Retry on a better connection, or with your VPN toggled; if you have to go through a proxy, tell the terminal about it with export HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:PORT (use your proxy app's port) and run pio run again

causes.cause: A download died halfway and left a corrupted partial file behind, so every retry trips over it
causes.check: Look in ~/.platformio/packages and ~/.platformio/.cache for odd temporary files
causes.fix: rm -rf ~/.platformio/.cache, delete the package folder named in the error from packages, then run again

causes.cause: Your office or school network blocks certain domains
causes.check: Try once on your phone's hotspot
causes.fix: Use the hotspot to finish the downloads (about 300MB, one time only). After that you don't need the network to build

entries.explain: The first time PlatformIO builds, it has to go pick up a toolbox from the warehouse: the compiler and the STM32 framework code. Once that toolbox is home in ~/.platformio, it never has to make the trip again.
entries.ask_ai: PlatformIO failed to download the toolchain on my first pio run. Error: [paste]. I'm on [home Wi-Fi / a corporate or school network / a VPN], [with a proxy on port PORT / no proxy]. Please tell me how to make pio use the proxy if needed, and how to clear the broken cache and retry.

entries.symptom: pio run says this isn't a PlatformIO project

causes.cause: Your terminal is in the wrong folder, not inside the project
causes.check: pwd shows where you are; ls shows whether platformio.ini is there
causes.fix: cd into the folder that contains platformio.ini and run again, or use pio run -d /path/to/project

causes.cause: The project was never initialized; all you have is a lone .cpp file
causes.check: ls to see whether platformio.ini and a src folder exist
causes.fix: pio project init --board bluepill_f103c8 creates the skeleton, then put your code in src/main.cpp

entries.explain: platformio.ini is the project's ID card. If pio can't find that card in the current folder, it has no idea whose project this is.
entries.ask_ai: pio run says Not a PlatformIO project. My pwd is [path] and ls shows: [paste]. Where should I be running this, or do I need to init first?

entries.symptom: During build or upload, macOS pops up saying a program is from an unidentified developer, or the process just gets killed
signals: cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified
is damaged and can't be opened

causes.cause: The toolchain binaries PlatformIO downloaded (arm-none-eabi-gcc, openocd) are being blocked by macOS Gatekeeper
causes.check: Open System Settings > Privacy & Security and scroll to the bottom for an "Open Anyway" prompt
causes.fix: Strip the quarantine flag from the whole folder: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine ~/.platformio/packages

causes.cause: You're on Apple Silicon running an Intel toolchain without Rosetta installed
causes.check: The error mentions Bad CPU type in executable
causes.fix: softwareupdate --install-rosetta --agree-to-license

entries.explain: macOS puts a "downloaded from the internet" sticker on every program you download, and you have to peel it off the first time you run it. The toolchain has dozens of little programs, each with its own sticker. Peeling them by hand would take forever; the command does them all at once.
entries.ask_ai: macOS is blocking PlatformIO's toolchain from running. Error: [paste]. My Mac has an [Intel / Apple Silicon] chip. How do I lift the block?

entries.symptom: The build says it can't find some .h header file
signals: fatal error: xxx.h: No such file or directory

causes.cause: The library isn't installed; it's not listed under lib_deps in platformio.ini
causes.check: cat platformio.ini and look for the library under lib_deps; ls .pio/libdeps/*/ shows what's actually installed
causes.fix: pio pkg search libraryname to find the exact name, add lib_deps = author/LibraryName to platformio.ini, then pio run again

causes.cause: The header filename is misspelled or has the wrong capitalization (macOS usually ignores case, but pio sometimes doesn't)
causes.check: Compare your #include line character by character against the one in the library's README
causes.fix: Change it to the exact name the library docs use

causes.cause: The library was written for ESP32/AVR and doesn't support STM32, so pio filtered it out
causes.check: Run pio run -v and look in the Library Dependency Finder section for a warning about compatible
causes.fix: Find an alternative library that lists STM32/ststm32 support; or set lib_compat_mode = off (it may still fail to build)

causes.cause: You just added lib_deps but haven't saved the file
causes.check: Look for an unsaved dot in your editor's title bar or tab
causes.fix: Save, then run again

entries.explain: #include is the dish you wrote down on your takeout order; lib_deps is what you actually paid for. Write the dish down without ordering it, and the kitchen can't bring it to you.
entries.ask_ai: STM32 Blue Pill + PlatformIO + Arduino framework. The build fails with fatal error: [filename].h: No such file or directory. My platformio.ini is: [paste]. Which library does this header belong to, and what should the lib_deps line say?

entries.symptom: I added the library to lib_deps, but pio says it can't find the package or can't resolve the version
signals: Could not find a version that satisfies

causes.cause: The library name isn't exact. In the pio registry, names look like author/LibraryName, not whatever people casually call it
causes.check: pio pkg search keyword and look at the exact names in the results
causes.fix: Copy the full name from the search results, for example adafruit/Adafruit SSD1306

causes.cause: Several libraries on one line separated by commas; pio only understands one per line
causes.check: Look for commas in your lib_deps line
causes.fix:
Put each library on its own indented line:
lib_deps =
    LibraryA
    LibraryB

causes.cause: An AI made up a library name that doesn't exist
causes.check: If pio pkg search can't find it, it was invented
causes.fix: Search https://registry.platformio.org by keyword yourself and use one that really exists

causes.cause: The version format is wrong, for example v1.2 or ==1.2
causes.check: Compare with the docs: the format is LibraryName@^1.2.0 or LibraryName@1.2.0
causes.fix: Drop the version number for now; worry about it once it builds

entries.explain: lib_deps is a shopping list you hand to pio, and every name has to match the label on the warehouse shelf exactly. One letter off, or a nickname instead of the real name, and the stock clerk comes back empty-handed.
entries.ask_ai: My platformio.ini lib_deps is: [paste], and pio reports [paste error]. Please check each library's exact name in the PlatformIO registry (flag any you're unsure about instead of guessing).

entries.symptom: The build spits out a wall of red saying expected something-or-other, or was not declared
signals: was not declared in this scope

causes.cause: A missing semicolon or a mismatched brace/parenthesis (usually on the line above; the error points at the next line)
causes.check: Look at the line number in the error, then look one or two lines up
causes.fix: Add the missing semicolon or brace. Put your cursor on a brace in the editor and it highlights the matching one; use that to count

causes.cause: A variable or function is used before it's defined, or spelled inconsistently (capitalization counts)
causes.check: Take the name from the was not declared error and search the whole file for where it's defined
causes.fix: Move the definition above where it's used, or add a function declaration at the top of the file

causes.cause: Code copied from a web page brought along curly quotes, odd punctuation, or invisible characters
causes.check: On the line that reports stray, delete the punctuation and retype it by hand
causes.fix: Retype the punctuation on that line by hand

causes.cause: undefined reference: a function is declared but never implemented, or the library only came with header files
causes.check: Search for the function name from the error and see whether it has a body with {}
causes.fix: Write the implementation; if it's a library function, make sure lib_deps installed the full library, not just a .h

entries.explain: The compiler is the world's most literal reader: one wrong punctuation mark and it refuses to read the rest of the paragraph. The location it reports is where it noticed the problem, not necessarily where the problem is. Look upward.
entries.ask_ai: STM32duino build error. Only the first error matters: [paste error with line number]. Here are the 5 lines before and after line [N]: [paste]. Please point to the exact character that's wrong. Don't rewrite the whole file.

entries.symptom: The last step of the build says region FLASH overflowed, or that it's out of memory
signals: Error: Program size is greater than maximum allowed

causes.cause: The libraries are too big. For example U8g2 with full fonts + floating-point printf + several large libraries won't fit in 64KB of Flash
causes.check: Look at the RAM/Flash usage percentages at the end of the build output
causes.fix: Switch to lighter libraries (U8g2 → U8x8, or use only one font); remove Serial.print calls you don't need; add -Os to build_flags

causes.cause: RAM overflow: you declared a huge array (like uint8_t buf[10000]) that won't fit in 20KB of RAM
causes.check: Search the code for [ followed by a big number ] to find large arrays
causes.fix: Make it smaller; mark lookup tables const so they live in Flash instead of RAM

causes.cause: Your chip actually has 128KB (many C8T6 chips do), but the board config assumes 64KB
causes.check: Only worth trying when you're just barely over
causes.fix: Change platformio.ini to board = bluepill_f103c8_128k (you must verify it actually runs after flashing; no guarantees)

entries.explain: The Blue Pill's Flash is a tiny 64KB hard drive and its RAM is a tiny 20KB desk. Your program is a file that has to fit on the drive; the variables it uses while running are papers spread out on the desk, and the desk is only so big.
entries.ask_ai: STM32F103C8T6 build fails with region FLASH overflowed by [N] bytes. The libraries I use are: [list lib_deps]. Please rank them by how much space they take, largest first, and suggest a lighter alternative for each.

entries.symptom: It builds fine but does nothing at all after flashing, or the build says the board doesn't exist

causes.cause: The board name is wrong, for example copied from the Arduino IDE
causes.check: cat platformio.ini and look at the board line
causes.fix: Change it to board = bluepill_f103c8, platform = ststm32, framework = arduino

causes.cause: framework is set to stm32cube or libopencm3, but the code is Arduino-style setup/loop
causes.check: Look at the framework line
causes.fix: framework = arduino

entries.explain: board tells the compiler which plot of land it's building on: how big it is and how the addresses are numbered. Get the plot wrong and however nice the house is, it's not on your land.
entries.ask_ai: I have an STM32F103C8T6 Blue Pill + ST-Link and want to use the Arduino framework. Please give me a minimal working platformio.ini (including upload_protocol) with a comment explaining each line.

entries.symptom: I changed the code but the board still does the old thing, or a weird build error won't go away no matter what I change

causes.cause: The editor didn't save, or you're editing a different copy of the file
causes.check: Add a line like Serial.println("v2") and see whether it shows up after flashing
causes.fix: Save; confirm the path you're editing is the same project path pio run is using

causes.cause: The incremental build cache got corrupted
causes.check: Run pio run -t clean, then pio run again
causes.fix: If clean doesn't help, rm -rf .pio and rebuild

causes.cause: The upload actually failed, but the message was buried under everything above it
causes.check: Scroll to the very end of the pio run -t upload output and look for SUCCESS or FAILED
causes.fix: Go to the Flashing section and troubleshoot there

entries.explain: To stay fast, pio only recompiles files that changed. Once in a while it misremembers which ones changed and assembles the new machine with old parts. clean tells it to forget everything and start over.
entries.ask_ai: I edited src/main.cpp but the behavior doesn't change after uploading. I've confirmed the file is saved. The full output of pio run -t upload is: [paste]. Please help me figure out whether it didn't compile, didn't upload, or uploaded the old firmware.

entries.symptom: I plugged in the ST-Link, but the upload says it can't find or open the device

causes.cause: macOS isn't seeing the ST-Link at all (bad USB cable, bad port, or a dead ST-Link)
causes.check: Run system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -i -A5 st-link, or open System Information > USB and look for STM32 STLink
causes.fix: Try a different USB port, a different cable, and plug in directly instead of through a hub. If it still doesn't show up, the ST-Link hardware is the problem

causes.cause: The ST-Link is recognized but the target board isn't wired up or powered (the error is usually about the target then; see the next entry)
causes.check: Is the LED on the ST-Link solid red (blue on some)? Is the board's power LED on?
causes.fix: Check the four wires: SWDIO, SWCLK, GND, 3.3V

causes.cause: Another program has the ST-Link open (STM32CubeProgrammer is running, or an openocd from another terminal never exited)
causes.check: ps aux | grep -i openocd to look for a leftover process
causes.fix: kill it, or unplug the ST-Link and plug it back in

causes.cause: platformio.ini doesn't have upload_protocol = stlink, so it defaulted to serial upload
causes.check: Does the error mention serial or /dev/cu.*?
causes.fix: Add the line upload_protocol = stlink

entries.explain: The ST-Link is the interpreter between your computer and the chip. "open failed" means the computer never even met the interpreter, so the chip isn't the issue yet. Fix the USB leg of the trip first.
entries.ask_ai: PlatformIO on macOS, uploading to an STM32F103 with an ST-Link V2, fails with [paste error]. The output of `system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -i -A8 stlink` is: [paste]. Please tell me whether the problem is on the USB side or the SWD side.

entries.symptom: The ST-Link is recognized, but the upload fails with unknown chip id or UNEXPECTED idcode

causes.cause: Your board has a compatible clone chip (CS32F103, GD32F103, APM32) and OpenOCD doesn't recognize its ID
causes.check: Look at the chip's printed markings with a magnifier or your phone camera: does it say STM32 or CS32/GD32/something else? An idcode of 0x2ba01477 in the error almost always means CS32
causes.fix: In platformio.ini add upload_flags = -c set CPUTAPID 0x2ba01477 (use the number from your error); sometimes debug_server needs the same argument

causes.cause: A counterfeit ST-Link (most of the $10 ones are) whose firmware doesn't play well with OpenOCD
causes.check: Try a different flashing tool: brew install stlink, then st-info --probe to see whether it can read the chip
causes.fix: If st-info sees it, flash the .bin with st-flash instead, or keep upload_protocol = stlink in platformio.ini and try a different openocd config

causes.cause: A loose SWD wire is producing a garbage ID
causes.check: Try a few times; if the ID is different every time, it's the wiring
causes.fix: Reseat the jumper wires, or swap them for new ones

entries.explain: Every chip leaves the factory with an ID number, and the programmer checks that ID before it does anything. Clone chips work the same but carry a different ID, so the programmer doesn't recognize it and refuses to proceed. You just tell it "this ID counts too."
entries.ask_ai: STM32 Blue Pill, uploading with an ST-Link, fails with UNEXPECTED idcode: [paste number]. The chip is marked [marking]. Please give me the exact upload_flags line for platformio.ini so OpenOCD accepts this ID.

entries.symptom: The ST-Link shows up, but it says it can't find the target chip or the target isn't responding
signals: Error: jtag status contains invalid mode value

causes.cause: One of the four SWD wires isn't connected properly: SWDIO, SWCLK, GND, 3.3V. A loose jumper wire or the wrong pin row
causes.check: Check the 4 pins on the top edge of the Blue Pill: left to right they're usually GND / SWCLK / SWDIO / 3V3, but go by the labels printed on the board, not the order. Same on the ST-Link side
causes.fix: Reconnect one wire at a time, matching the printed labels; try a fresh set of jumper wires

causes.cause: The board has no power. You wired SWDIO/SWCLK/GND but not 3.3V, and the board isn't plugged into USB either
causes.check: Is the board's power LED (PWR) on?
causes.fix: Connect the ST-Link's 3.3V to the board's 3V3, or power the board over USB (and in that case don't also connect the ST-Link's 3.3V)

causes.cause: SWDIO and SWCLK are swapped
causes.check: Swap the two wires and try again
causes.fix: Swap them

causes.cause: The previous program turned PA13/PA14 into ordinary GPIO pins, which disabled the SWD port
causes.check: Hold the board's RESET button, start the upload, and release RESET right as it starts. If it connects, this is it
causes.fix: Add -c reset_config srst_only srst_nogate connect_assert_srst to upload_flags, and wire the ST-Link's RST to the board's R pin

entries.explain: The interpreter (ST-Link) showed up, but the phone call to the chip isn't going through. Either a wire isn't seated or the chip has no power at all. SWD is just two signal wires plus ground and power, so the problem is almost always in those four wires.
entries.ask_ai: Blue Pill + ST-Link V2 upload fails with target not found. My wiring: [list which ST-Link pin goes to which board pin]. The board's PWR LED is [on/off]. Please check my wiring and give me the upload_flags for using the RST pin.

entries.symptom: The upload succeeds but the program doesn't run; or when flashing over serial (no ST-Link) it never connects

causes.cause: The BOOT0 jumper is in the 1 position, so after reset the chip boots into the factory bootloader instead of your program
causes.check: Look at the two yellow jumpers on the board; is the one next to the BOOT0 label on the 0 side or the 1 side?
causes.fix: For ST-Link uploads: BOOT0=0 and BOOT1=0, both toward the edge of the board. Press RESET after flashing

causes.cause: When flashing over serial (USB-TTL), BOOT0 has to be moved to 1 and the board reset before flashing, then moved back to 0 afterward
causes.check: Are you flashing with a CH340 on PA9/PA10 instead of an ST-Link?
causes.fix: Before flashing: BOOT0=1, press RESET. After flashing: BOOT0=0, press RESET. It's a hassle; just use the ST-Link and never touch the jumpers

entries.explain: BOOT0 is a startup switch: 0 = start from the program you flashed, 1 = start from the tiny factory program built into the chip (which exists just to receive serial uploads). If you're using an ST-Link, leave this switch on 0 forever.
entries.ask_ai: I'm not sure where the two BOOT jumpers on my Blue Pill should go. I'm flashing with [an ST-Link / a USB-to-serial adapter]. Please tell me which side BOOT0 and BOOT1 should each be on, and whether I need to move them after a successful upload.

entries.symptom: It connects, but the write fails and says the chip is protected

causes.cause: Readout protection (RDP) was enabled at the factory or by a previous owner; common on used or salvaged chips
causes.check: If the error contains protected, this is it
causes.fix: Unlocking wipes the entire Flash, which is fine here. In platformio.ini add -c "init; reset halt; stm32f1x unlock 0; reset halt" to upload_flags, run once, then remove it and flash normally. Or use st-flash --reset erase or STM32CubeProgrammer to clear RDP

causes.cause: The last upload was interrupted (cable yanked) and the Flash is stuck half-locked
causes.check: Hold RESET and retry the upload
causes.fix: Same as above: unlock plus a full chip erase

entries.explain: The chip has an anti-copy lock. Once it's on, outsiders can neither read nor write. The only way to open the lock is to destroy everything inside, which costs you nothing since you're about to flash something new anyway.
entries.ask_ai: Flashing an STM32F103 fails with device protected / RDP. I'm using PlatformIO + ST-Link. Please give me a single openocd or st-flash command I can run in the macOS terminal to remove readout protection and erase the whole chip.

entries.symptom: The power LED comes on when I plug in USB, but my Mac doesn't see any device at all (no ST-Link, no serial port)
signals: not in the USB device list

causes.cause: It's a charge-only USB cable with just two power wires and no data wires (the cables that come with power banks and desk fans are usually like this)
causes.check: Swap in a cable you know carries data (like the one that came with your phone and can sync photos to a computer)
causes.fix: Replace the cable. Keep one cable labeled "data" just for this

causes.cause: The USB-C adapter or hub doesn't pass data, or can't supply enough power
causes.check: Remove the adapter and plug straight into the Mac
causes.fix: Use a powered hub, or plug in directly

causes.cause: The Blue Pill's onboard micro USB port can't be used for flashing (there's no USB bootloader from the factory); it's power only
causes.check: Are you trying to flash through the board's own USB port?
causes.fix: This is normal. Flash with the ST-Link, do serial with a CH340 on PA9/PA10, and treat the board's USB port as a power plug

entries.explain: A USB cable has four wires: two carry power, two carry data. Cheap cables leave out the data wires. The LED still lights up, but the computer hears nothing. A lit LED proves there's power, not that there's communication.
entries.ask_ai: My STM32 board's power LED comes on over USB but macOS doesn't recognize anything (nothing in system_profiler SPUSBDataType). I'm using [the board's USB port / an ST-Link / a CH340]. Please list the likely causes in order of probability, each with a one-minute check.

entries.symptom: I plugged in the CH340 serial adapter, but nothing like cu.usbserial or cu.wchusbserial shows up in /dev

causes.cause: Charge-only cable (see the previous entry)
causes.check: Run system_profiler SPUSBDataType | grep -i -B2 -A8 'ch34\|1a86'. If there's an entry, USB sees it and the problem is the driver; if not, it's the cable
causes.fix: Use a data cable

causes.cause: macOS 12+ has a built-in CH340 driver, but some knockoff CH340 chips need the official WCH driver
causes.check: USB sees the device in the previous step, but nothing shows up in /dev
causes.fix: Download CH34xVCPDriver for macOS from WCH's website, install it, allow it in System Settings > Privacy & Security, then restart

causes.cause: It's actually a CP2102 or FT232, not a CH340; you misidentified the chip
causes.check: Read the chip marking on the adapter
causes.fix: CP2102 is supported natively on macOS and shows up as cu.usbserial-xxxx or cu.SLAB_USBtoUART; FT232 shows up as cu.usbserial-xxxx

entries.explain: When you plug in a serial adapter, the Mac needs the matching instruction manual (the driver) before it can assign it an address like /dev/cu.*. Recent macOS ships with most manuals built in, but counterfeit chips sometimes need a special one.
entries.ask_ai: On macOS, plugging in a CH340 USB-to-serial adapter doesn't add anything to /dev/cu.*. The relevant part of `system_profiler SPUSBDataType` is: [paste]. macOS version: [version]. Please tell me whether it's the cable, the driver, or the hardware.

entries.symptom: The upload runs all the way through, then says verify failed or the checksum doesn't match

causes.cause: The SWD wires are too long or loose, so the data got corrupted on the way in
causes.check: Retry with shorter wires (under 6 inches / 15cm)
causes.fix: Swap the wires; add -c "adapter speed 1000" to upload_flags to slow things down

causes.cause: A counterfeit ST-Link that's unstable at high speed
causes.check: It works once you slow it down
causes.fix: Pin adapter speed at 1000, or even 500

causes.cause: Bad Flash blocks (very rare)
causes.check: Compare with another board
causes.fix: Replace the board

entries.explain: After flashing, the programmer reads everything back to compare answers. A mismatch means words got dropped in transit. It's like dictating over a long, crackly phone line: speak slower and it comes through cleaner.
entries.ask_ai: Flashing an STM32 with an ST-Link fails with verify failed / checksum mismatch. Please give me the upload_flags line for platformio.ini that lowers the SWD speed.

entries.symptom: The upload says SUCCESS, but the onboard LED doesn't blink and nothing happens

causes.cause: The code uses LED_BUILTIN or some pin other than PC13
causes.check: Search the code for the pin name in pinMode; the Blue Pill's onboard LED is on PC13
causes.fix: Change it to pinMode(PC13, OUTPUT). PC13 is active-low: digitalWrite(PC13, LOW) turns it on

causes.cause: The chip wasn't reset after flashing and is still parked in debug mode
causes.check: Press the RESET button on the board
causes.fix: Press RESET; add upload_flags = -c "reset run" to platformio.ini, or wire the ST-Link's RST line so it resets automatically

causes.cause: The BOOT0 jumper is on 1 (see boot_jumper_wrong in the Flashing section)
causes.check: Look at the jumpers
causes.fix: Move BOOT0 to 0 and press RESET

causes.cause: The delay is way too short or way too long (like delay(1) or delay(100000))
causes.check: Look at the number inside delay in loop
causes.fix: delay(500)

entries.explain: A successful upload only means the program landed on the chip's hard drive, not that it's running the right thing. There are three layers to an LED that won't blink: the program never started (reset/BOOT), the program is running but controlling a different LED (pin), or it's controlling this LED but with the logic backwards (PC13 lights on LOW).
entries.ask_ai: Blue Pill STM32F103C8T6, PlatformIO with the Arduino framework. The upload says SUCCESS but the onboard LED doesn't blink. Code: [paste]. BOOT0 is on [0/1], and I [have / have not] pressed RESET. Please tell me what to check first, in order.

entries.symptom: Writing HIGH turns the LED off and LOW turns it on, the opposite of what the tutorial says

causes.cause: The Blue Pill's onboard LED has one leg on 3.3V and the other on PC13; current only flows when PC13 outputs LOW
causes.check: If digitalWrite(PC13, LOW) lights it, everything is working as designed
causes.fix: This isn't a bug. Just write LOW to mean on, or define #define LED_ON LOW

entries.explain: Think of the LED as a faucet with one end hooked to a water tower (3.3V). Water only flows when the PC13 end is lowered (to ground). Raise it to the same height (also 3.3V) and nothing moves. Tutorials usually wire an external LED the other way around, which is why HIGH means on there.
entries.ask_ai: Why does the Blue Pill's onboard LED on PC13 only light when I write LOW? If I want to wire an external LED to PA0 so that HIGH turns it on, how do I connect it? Describe the wiring and tell me what resistor value to use.

entries.symptom: The program runs while the ST-Link is connected, but as soon as I unplug it and power the board from USB alone, nothing happens
signals: stops when I unplug the ST-Link

causes.cause: The code starts with while(!Serial); waiting for a USB serial connection, so without a computer on the serial port it waits forever
causes.check: Search the code for while (!Serial)
causes.fix: Delete that line, or give it a timeout: unsigned long t=millis(); while(!Serial && millis()-t<2000);

causes.cause: The BOOT0 jumper is on 1, so a reset lands in the bootloader (the ST-Link can force the program to run during upload, but a reset can't)
causes.check: Look at the jumper
causes.fix: BOOT0=0

causes.cause: Unstable USB power or a bad cable, so the board never actually starts
causes.check: Is the PWR LED on? Try another USB port
causes.fix: Swap the cable or the port

entries.explain: The program is standing at the front door waiting for a "the computer is connected to serial" signal before it does anything, like a security guard who won't open up until you badge in. With no computer attached, nobody ever badges in, and the program waits outside forever.
entries.ask_ai: My STM32 Blue Pill program works with the ST-Link attached but not on USB power alone. The start of the code is: [paste the first 15 lines up to and including setup()]. Please check whether anything is blocking while waiting for the serial port.

entries.symptom: The board feels hot to the touch, or one chip is too hot to keep my finger on

causes.cause: The 3.3V regulator (the small flat chip on the board) is carrying a heavy load, like a servo or a display drawing from the 3V3 pin
causes.check: Unplug every peripheral so only the bare board is left. Still hot?
causes.fix: Move peripherals to 5V or their own power supply; 3V3 should only feed the STM32 and small sensors

causes.cause: A pin is shorted to GND or to power (jumper wires touching, wrong row on the breadboard)
causes.check: Cut power immediately. Look for two wires plugged into the same breadboard column
causes.fix: Power off and rewire

causes.cause: 5V was connected straight into the 3V3 pin
causes.check: Retrace your wiring: which pin did the power go to?
causes.fix: Power off. 5V only goes to the pin labeled 5V. The chip may already be damaged; reflash and test

causes.cause: A GPIO pin is driving a motor or relay directly (see the Actuators section)
causes.check: Is anything motor-like connected straight to a GPIO pin?
causes.fix: Disconnect it and add a driver

entries.explain: Slightly warm is normal; too hot to touch means too much current is flowing somewhere. Electricity is like water: wherever it's leaking, that's where it gets hot. Your first move is to cut power, then investigate. Don't "watch it a little longer."
entries.ask_ai: My STM32 Blue Pill is getting very hot at [location]. I have these things connected: [list peripherals and which pin each is on]. I've already cut power. Please help me figure out which connection is the most likely culprit, and how to test whether the chip is damaged.

entries.symptom: The program runs for a bit, then restarts on its own; the serial output keeps repeating whatever's in setup

causes.cause: Not enough power. The moment a peripheral does something (servo moves, motor starts, display refreshes), the voltage sags and the chip resets
causes.check: Unplug the power-hungry peripherals and see if it still resets
causes.fix: Give peripherals their own power supply and share a common ground; add a 100uF or larger capacitor across the power rails

causes.cause: An array out of bounds or a null pointer in the code sends the program into a HardFault, which resets it
causes.check: What's the last line the serial output printed before the crash? That points to the code region
causes.fix: Check the array indexes and pointers in that region

causes.cause: The watchdog (IWDG) is enabled but never fed
causes.check: Search the code for IWatchdog
causes.fix: Call IWatchdog.reload() regularly in loop, or remove it for now

entries.explain: The chip has a low-voltage protection circuit that reboots it whenever the voltage dips below a threshold. A motor starting up is like someone opening a big faucet on the same pipe: your water pressure drops for an instant, the chip gets "starved" for a moment, and it restarts.
entries.ask_ai: My STM32 program keeps restarting. The serial output pattern is: [paste]. Peripherals: [list]. Power comes from [USB / other]. Please help me decide whether it's a power problem or a code problem, with one test for each.

entries.symptom: delay timing is off: a 1-second blink takes 8 seconds, or the serial timestamps look weird

causes.cause: A clone chip or clone board whose crystal doesn't match the default clock configuration
causes.check: Write a program that blinks once per second and time 10 blinks with your phone's stopwatch
causes.fix: Confirm board = bluepill_f103c8; add -D HSE_VALUE=8000000U to build_flags (the crystal on the board is marked 8.000)

causes.cause: delayMicroseconds was given a number too large and overflowed
causes.check: Anything above 16383 is inaccurate
causes.fix: Use delay() for anything longer than 16ms

entries.explain: The chip keeps time with a metronome (the crystal). If the metronome's actual speed doesn't match what the program thinks it is, everything time-related runs proportionally fast or slow.
entries.ask_ai: On my STM32F103 Blue Pill, delay(1000) actually takes [N] seconds. The crystal on the board is marked [marking]. Please give me the platformio.ini line to set HSE_VALUE, and a way to verify the clock is right.

entries.symptom: The serial monitor is full of gibberish: question marks, boxes, random symbols

causes.cause: Baud rate mismatch: the code says Serial.begin(115200) but the monitor is at 9600 (or the other way around)
causes.check: Compare the number in Serial.begin with the -b argument of pio device monitor
causes.fix: Add monitor_speed = 115200 to platformio.ini, matching the code

causes.cause: A wrong clock is skewing the actual baud rate (see millis_delay_weird)
causes.check: Is the LED blink timing also off?
causes.fix: Fix the clock first

causes.cause: Only the first few characters are garbage and then it's fine: that's noise from the moment of reset
causes.check: Only the first line or two are garbled
causes.fix: This is normal. Adding delay(100) before Serial.begin in setup helps a bit

entries.explain: The baud rate is the talking speed both sides agree on. If you talk at 115200 and the other side listens at 9600, all it hears is static. Make the two numbers match and it clears up.
entries.ask_ai: My STM32duino serial output is all gibberish. The code has Serial.begin([number]), and monitor_speed in platformio.ini is [number or not set]. I'm using [PA9/PA10 to a CH340 / the onboard USB]. Please tell me where the mismatch is.

entries.symptom: The serial monitor shows nothing at all, completely blank, and I've confirmed the baud rate is right

causes.cause: TX is wired to TX and RX to RX. It should be board TX (PA9) → adapter RX, and board RX (PA10) → adapter TX
causes.check: Look at the wiring. TX to TX is wrong
causes.fix: Swap the TX and RX wires

causes.cause: The code uses Serial, but in STM32duino Serial may default to USB CDC (the onboard USB port), not PA9/PA10
causes.check: You have a CH340 on PA9/PA10: does the code say Serial or Serial1?
causes.fix: Use Serial1.begin() for PA9/PA10, or add build_flags = -D SERIAL_UART_INSTANCE=1 to platformio.ini

causes.cause: No common ground. The CH340's GND isn't connected to the board's GND
causes.check: Count the wires between the CH340 and the board: you need at least 3 (TX, RX, GND)
causes.fix: Connect GND

causes.cause: The monitor opened the wrong port
causes.check: ls /dev/cu.* to see how many there are; pio device list
causes.fix: Add monitor_port = /dev/cu.wchusbserialXXXX to platformio.ini

entries.explain: TX is a mouth, RX is an ear. For two people to talk, mouth goes to ear; mouth to mouth and nobody hears anything. GND is the shared reference line; without it, the two sides can't even agree on what "high" and "low" mean.
entries.ask_ai: Blue Pill + CH340, and the serial monitor shows nothing. Wiring: board [pin] → CH340 [pin] ([N] wires total). The code uses Serial[number].begin. Please check whether the wiring and the Serial instance match.

entries.symptom: Serial works on and off: a few characters here and there, or it changes when I touch a wire

causes.cause: No common ground, or the ground wire has a bad connection
causes.check: Unplug and reseat the GND-to-GND wire, or replace it
causes.fix: Make sure there's a solid physical wire between the CH340's GND and the board's GND

causes.cause: A broken jumper wire (snapped inside; it looks fine from the outside)
causes.check: Swap the wire
causes.fix: Throw the suspect wire away. Don't keep it around

entries.explain: Each device has its own idea of "zero volts." If you don't tie them together, what one side calls 3.3V might look like 1V or 5V to the other, depending on luck. The ground wire lines up the two zeros.
entries.ask_ai: My serial output works intermittently. I have [N] wires connected: [list]. Please confirm whether I'm missing a common ground, and give me a one-minute test to tell wiring problems from everything else.

entries.symptom: Opening the serial monitor says the port is in use / resource busy

causes.cause: Another terminal or program still has the port open (a pio device monitor you never closed, the Arduino IDE, screen)
causes.check: lsof | grep cu.usb or lsof | grep wchusb to see who has it
causes.fix: Close that program; if you can't find it, kill the PID lsof lists; failing that, unplug and replug the USB

causes.cause: Upload and monitor are both open and fighting over the same port (when flashing over serial)
causes.check: Are you flashing over serial?
causes.fix: Ctrl+C to close the monitor before uploading

entries.explain: A serial port is a one-lane bridge: only one program can be on it at a time. If the last program never got off the bridge, the next one has to wait.
entries.ask_ai: pio device monitor on macOS reports Resource busy. The output of `lsof | grep -i usb` is: [paste]. Please tell me how to free up the port.

entries.symptom: pio device list doesn't show my serial port, or shows a bunch and I can't tell which is mine

causes.cause: Only the built-in Bluetooth ports are listed, which means your device was never recognized (cable or driver; see the Flashing section)
causes.check: Unplug the serial adapter and run ls /dev/cu.*, plug it in and run it again; the new one is yours
causes.fix: Put that new name into monitor_port

causes.cause: The ST-Link doesn't provide a serial port, and you're trying to use it as one
causes.check: Is the ST-Link the only thing plugged in?
causes.fix: The ST-Link V2 (the little white USB-stick style one) has no serial function. You need a separate CH340 on PA9/PA10

causes.cause: You want to use the onboard USB as a serial port but USB CDC isn't enabled
causes.check: Does platformio.ini have -D USBCON -D USBD_USE_CDC?
causes.fix: Add -D PIO_FRAMEWORK_ARDUINO_ENABLE_CDC -D USBCON -D USBD_VID=0x0483 -D USBD_PID=0x5740 to build_flags. Note the onboard USB pull-up resistor is often wrong (R10 is 10K instead of 1.5K), so it may not work at all

entries.explain: /dev/cu.* is the list of every serial "street address" on your Mac. The Bluetooth ones are permanent residents that come with the system. When you plug in your device, a new address should appear. If it doesn't, the device never made it through the door.
entries.ask_ai: On macOS, `ls /dev/cu.*` shows: [paste]. I have [an ST-Link / a CH340 / the board's USB] plugged in. Which one is my serial port? If none of them, what's the most likely reason?

entries.symptom: Printing a decimal number only shows the whole part or a question mark; printing special characters (accents, the ° symbol, emoji) comes out garbled

causes.cause: You used Serial.printf("%f") but floating-point formatting isn't enabled by default
causes.check: Try Serial.println(x, 2) instead and see whether the decimals show up
causes.fix: Use Serial.print(x, 2); or add -Wl,-u,_printf_float to build_flags (costs a few KB of Flash)

causes.cause: Garbled special characters: the terminal and source file use different encodings, or the monitor doesn't handle UTF-8
causes.check: Try pio device monitor instead (it defaults to UTF-8)
causes.fix: Make sure the source file is saved as UTF-8; add monitor_filters = default, time to platformio.ini; while debugging, stick to plain ASCII

entries.explain: To save space, the embedded printf leaves out the "print decimals" module by default, and you have to switch it on. It's like buying a printer that ships without the color cartridge.
entries.ask_ai: In STM32duino, Serial.printf("%f") won't print decimals. Please give me the solution that costs the least Flash, plus the build_flags version.

entries.symptom: I press the button once and the counter jumps by several, or the LED state flickers randomly

causes.cause: A mechanical button bounces for a few milliseconds when pressed, and the program sees dozens of high/low transitions
causes.check: Serial.println every value you read after pressing the button and see whether it's a string of 0101
causes.fix: Software debounce: after detecting a change, delay(20) and read again to confirm; or record the time of the last change with millis() and ignore anything within 50ms

causes.cause: No pull-up, so the pin floats and flips randomly (see gpio_floating)
causes.check: Is the reading stable when you're not touching the button?
causes.fix: pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP)

causes.cause: You're mixing up "was just pressed" with "is being held," so every pass through loop counts again
causes.check: Hold the button down; if the count keeps climbing, this is it
causes.fix: Remember the previous state and only count when it goes from not-pressed to pressed (edge detection)

entries.explain: When the metal contacts inside a button meet, they bounce like a ping-pong ball, making and breaking contact several times within a few milliseconds. To you it feels like one press; the chip, checking every microsecond, sees several. Debouncing just means "when you see a change, wait a beat and confirm."
entries.ask_ai: STM32duino, button on [pin], one press counts multiple times. Please give me non-blocking debounce plus edge-detection code using millis(), with INPUT_PULLUP and the button wired to GND.

entries.symptom: When I'm not pressing the button, the reading changes randomly, and it changes when my hand gets close
signals: changes when my hand is near

causes.cause: The pin is set to INPUT with no pull-up or pull-down, so when the button is released the pin is connected to nothing (floating) and picks up interference like an antenna
causes.check: Does the pinMode line say INPUT instead of INPUT_PULLUP?
causes.fix: Change it to INPUT_PULLUP, with one side of the button on the pin and the other on GND. Now pressed = LOW

causes.cause: You have a pull-up but the other side of the button goes to 3.3V instead of GND, so pressing it just shorts the pull-up
causes.check: Where does the other side of the button go?
causes.fix: Pull-up pairs with GND, pull-down pairs with VCC; pick one

entries.explain: A wire connected to nothing is an antenna. Your phone, the lights, your own hand all induce voltage on it. A pull-up resistor is like a thin string gently holding the pin up at 3.3V; pressing the button yanks it firmly down to GND.
entries.ask_ai: My STM32 button reading floats and flips randomly. My pinMode is [INPUT/INPUT_PULLUP], and the button is wired to [pin] and [GND/3.3V]. Please give me the correct wiring and code, and tell me whether a press reads HIGH or LOW.

entries.symptom: Pressed reads 0 and released reads 1, backwards from what I expected

causes.cause: You're using INPUT_PULLUP with the button to GND, so pressed is LOW. That's the correct and recommended wiring
causes.check: Look at pinMode
causes.fix: No hardware change needed. In code, if (digitalRead(pin) == LOW) means pressed; or bool pressed = !digitalRead(pin)

entries.explain: With a pull-up, "pressed = grounded = 0" is the default convention in electronics, not a mistake. It's like light switches in some countries where down means on. Get used to it, or flip it once with a variable.
entries.ask_ai: Why does a button wired with INPUT_PULLUP read LOW when pressed? Please write me an isPressed() function that hides the inverted logic.

entries.symptom: I connected a 5V sensor's output to an STM32 pin and I'm worried I fried it (or already did)

causes.cause: Most of the Blue Pill's digital pins are 5V-tolerant (FT), but the ADC pins like PA0-PA7 and PB0/PB1 are not
causes.check: Look up the pin in bluepill-pins.json and see whether it has the FT tag
causes.fix: Connect 5V digital signals to FT pins (like PB5-PB15, PA8-PA15); anything going to an ADC pin must be divided down to below 3.3V

causes.cause: The pin is configured as OUTPUT but also has an external voltage on it
causes.check: Look at pinMode
causes.fix: Any pin that receives an external signal must be INPUT

entries.explain: The chip is a 3.3V chip. Some pins wear a raincoat that lets them survive 5V (FT); others don't. None of the ADC pins have one, so putting 5V on them is like pouring boiling water on bare skin.
entries.ask_ai: I want to connect the 5V output of a [sensor name] to an STM32F103C8T6. Please tell me which pins are 5V-tolerant, and if I have to use an ADC pin, what resistor values to use for a voltage divider.

entries.symptom: The servo jitters, buzzes, and won't hold its position

causes.cause: Not enough power. The servo is drawing from the board's 3V3 or from USB 5V, which can't supply the current; every time the voltage dips the servo re-seeks its position
causes.check: Power the servo from a separate 5V supply (4 AA batteries or a 5V 2A adapter) with GND tied to the board's GND
causes.fix: Separate power plus common ground; the signal wire still goes to the board

causes.cause: Loose jumper wires on the signal or power lines
causes.check: Pinch the connectors and see if the jitter changes
causes.fix: Swap the wires, or solder

causes.cause: loop runs too fast and keeps writing the same angle, or the delay is too short
causes.check: Write the angle once, then delay(2000). Still jittering?
causes.fix: Only call write when the angle changes

causes.cause: Cheap servos (SG90) have a tiny deadband and hunt back and forth once they arrive
causes.check: Compare with another servo
causes.fix: Call servo.detach() after it arrives to cut the signal

entries.explain: A servo is like a hungry weightlifter who gulps power every time it moves. The board's 3V3 is a thin cocktail straw that can't keep up, so the servo starts shaking. Give it its own fat hose (separate power supply), then tie the grounds together so everyone agrees on where zero is.
entries.ask_ai: An SG90 servo on my STM32 Blue Pill [pin] is jittering. The servo gets power from [the board's 3V3 / the board's 5V / a separate supply]. Please describe the correct power wiring in text and give me minimal code using the Servo library.

entries.symptom: The servo doesn't move at all and doesn't make a sound

causes.cause: The signal wire is on a pin with no timer PWM, or one the Servo library doesn't support
causes.check: Try PA8 or PB6
causes.fix: Use a pin with a TIM alternate function: PA0-PA3, PA6-PA10, PB0/PB1, PB6-PB9. Check bluepill-pins.json

causes.cause: The servo's three wires are mixed up: brown/black = GND, red = 5V, orange/yellow = signal
causes.check: Match the colors
causes.fix: Rewire by color

causes.cause: No power, or only 3.3V (most servos need 4.8V or more)
causes.check: Is the red wire on 5V or 3V3?
causes.fix: Connect it to 5V

causes.cause: The code calls attach but never write, or writes the angle it's already at
causes.check: Write a loop that goes 0 → 90 → 180
causes.fix: Fix the code

entries.explain: A servo needs three things: enough power, the right ground, and a signal wire that gets a pulse every 20ms. Missing any one and it won't budge. Check power and ground first (multimeter, or swap in an LED), then check whether the signal pin can actually produce PWM.
entries.ask_ai: A servo on my Blue Pill [pin], powered from [where], doesn't move at all. Code: [paste]. Please first confirm whether this pin works with the Servo library in STM32duino, then check the wiring.

entries.symptom: analogWrite does nothing: the LED doesn't dim, it's either fully on or fully off

causes.cause: The pin has no timer output (for example PC13, PC14, PC15, PA13/PA14)
causes.check: Try PA8 or PB6
causes.fix: Use a pin with a TIMx_CHy function (check bluepill-pins.json)

causes.cause: No pinMode(pin, OUTPUT) (STM32duino's analogWrite sometimes does this automatically, sometimes not)
causes.check: Add the pinMode
causes.fix: Add it

causes.cause: The value range is wrong; the default is 0-255, so writing 1023 is just fully on
causes.check: Try analogWrite(pin, 30) and see whether it dims
causes.fix: Stay within 0-255; for 12-bit use analogWriteResolution(12)

entries.explain: PWM switches the LED on and off so fast your eye sees it as half-bright. The part of the chip that can do this is a timer, but timers are only wired to some of the pins. Pins without one can only be on or off.
entries.ask_ai: STM32F103C8T6 with STM32duino: which pins support analogWrite (PWM)? I want to connect [N] LEDs and [N] servos. Please assign pins for me and avoid timer conflicts.

entries.symptom: The buzzer plays the wrong pitch, the motor squeals, or I can visibly see the LED flickering

causes.cause: The PWM frequency is too low (default 1kHz): motors are audible at that rate and LEDs flicker up close
causes.check: Try analogWriteFrequency(20000)
causes.fix: Use 20kHz or higher for motors; 1kHz is fine for LEDs; for buzzers use tone(pin, frequency)

causes.cause: A passive buzzer driven with digitalWrite just clicks once; it needs a square wave
causes.check: Does tone(pin, 1000) make a sound?
causes.fix: Use tone()/noTone()

entries.explain: The speed PWM switches at is its "pitch." 1000 times a second is within human hearing, and the motor's coils will sing it right at you. Push it up to 20000 times a second and it's above what anyone can hear.
entries.ask_ai: How do I set the analogWrite PWM frequency in STM32duino? I'm driving a [motor/buzzer/LED] on [pin] and I want [no noise / the correct pitch].

entries.symptom: analogRead keeps jumping around, and there's a reading even with nothing connected
signals: reads a value with nothing connected

causes.cause: The pin is floating and you're reading noise out of thin air. That's normal
causes.check: Jumper the pin to GND: the reading should be near 0. To 3V3: near 4095
causes.fix: Connect the actual sensor and look again; readings from a floating pin are meaningless

causes.cause: The sensor signal itself is noisy (potentiometer contact, long wires)
causes.check: Read 16 times in a row and average
causes.fix: Average multiple samples; shorten the signal wire; add a 0.1uF capacitor on the sensor's power

causes.cause: Dirty power (USB supply fluctuating)
causes.check: Unplug other power-hungry peripherals and see if it improves
causes.fix: Add a 10uF capacitor between 3V3 and GND; when the reference voltage wobbles, every reading drifts with it

causes.cause: You assumed 0-1023, but the STM32 is 12-bit: 0-4095
causes.check: Connect to 3V3 and see whether the max is 4095
causes.fix: Convert using 4095: voltage = reading / 4095.0 * 3.3

entries.explain: The ADC is an extremely fine ruler; point it at empty air and it still gives you a number. Unstable doesn't mean broken; it means the thing you're measuring is moving. Take several readings and average them, like standing still on a bathroom scale before you read it.
entries.ask_ai: STM32F103 analogRead([pin]) reading a [sensor] jumps around by ±[N]. Please give me moving-average filter code and tell me how much jitter is normal.

entries.symptom: My sensor outputs 0-5V and the ADC reading is pinned at the max, or I'm worried about frying the pin

causes.cause: The STM32 ADC can only measure up to 3.3V. Feed it 5V and it reads full scale every time, and over time it damages the pin (ADC pins are not 5V-tolerant)
causes.check: Look up the output range in the sensor's datasheet
causes.fix: Voltage divider: signal → 10K → ADC pin → 20K → GND (turns 5V into 3.33V, which is cutting it close; 10K/15K gives a safer 3V). Multiply back by the ratio when you convert

causes.cause: The sensor is powered from 5V but its signal is actually 3.3V logic, so it's fine
causes.check: Find the output voltage line in the datasheet
causes.fix: No divider needed; connect directly

entries.explain: The ADC's ruler only goes up to 3.3V. Measure something at 5V and all it can say is "off the end of the ruler." A voltage divider shrinks 5V proportionally so it fits on the ruler, and you scale it back up after reading.
entries.ask_ai: I have a [sensor] that outputs 0-5V and want to connect it to an STM32F103 ADC. Please give me the voltage divider resistor values and wiring, plus the formula to convert the analogRead value back to the original voltage.

entries.symptom: The voltage I calculate doesn't match my multimeter; everything reads consistently high or low

causes.cause: The board's 3V3 isn't actually 3.3V (on USB power it's often 3.2-3.3V), but your formula assumes 3.3
causes.check: Measure between the board's 3V3 and GND pins with a multimeter
causes.fix: Use the measured value in your formula; or read the internal reference with analogRead(AVREF) and correct dynamically

causes.cause: The resolution is set to 10-bit but you're dividing by 4095 (or the reverse)
causes.check: Search for analogReadResolution
causes.fix: Keep them consistent: the default is 12-bit → 4095

entries.explain: The ADC uses the voltage on the 3V3 pin as its yardstick. If the yardstick itself is 5% short, every measurement comes out 5% off.
entries.ask_ai: The voltage I calculate from my STM32F103 ADC readings is [N]% off from my multimeter. The board's 3V3 pin measures [voltage]. Please fix my formula and explain how to auto-correct using the internal VREFINT.

entries.symptom: The I2C scanner program doesn't find a single address

causes.cause: SDA/SCL are swapped or on the wrong pins. The Blue Pill's default I2C1 is SCL=PB6, SDA=PB7
causes.check: Match the labels on the module: SDA→PB7, SCL→PB6
causes.fix: Rewire; or tell the code where they are with Wire.setSDA(PB9); Wire.setSCL(PB8); if that's where you connected them

causes.cause: The module has no power or the wrong voltage (some OLEDs need 5V, others only take 3.3V)
causes.check: Where is the module's VCC connected? Does the module have a power LED or a regulator chip?
causes.fix: Check the module's documentation; when in doubt, start with 3.3V

causes.cause: No pull-up resistors. Most modules include them, but bare chips and some cheap modules don't
causes.check: Look on the back of the module for small resistors marked 4.7K or 10K
causes.fix: Add a 4.7K from SDA to 3.3V and another from SCL to 3.3V

causes.cause: No common ground
causes.check: Count the wires: VCC, GND, SDA, SCL, all four
causes.fix: Connect GND

causes.cause: The scanner program prints to Serial but you're connected to Serial1, so you never see the output
causes.check: Does the scanner print Scanning... at the start?
causes.fix: See the Serial section

entries.explain: I2C is a two-wire bus route: every device hangs off the same two wires and has its own street address. Scanning means calling out each address and listening for a reply. If nobody answers, the wires are usually wrong or the bus (power) isn't running.
entries.ask_ai: STM32 Blue Pill I2C scanner finds no devices. Wiring: module SDA→[pin], SCL→[pin], VCC→[voltage], GND→GND. The module is a [model]. Please check my pins and give me an I2C scanner program for STM32duino.

entries.symptom: The scanner finds an address, but the library fails to initialize / the display stays dark

causes.cause: The library's default address doesn't match the actual one. OLEDs are usually 0x3C (some 0x3D); LCD1602 backpacks are usually 0x27 (some 0x3F)
causes.check: Compare the address the scanner found with the argument to begin() in your code
causes.fix: Plug in the scanned address: display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, 0x3C) / LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2)

causes.cause: SSD1306 allocation failed means you're out of RAM, not that the address is wrong
causes.check: Look at the RAM usage in the build output
causes.fix: Shrink other arrays, or switch to a library like U8x8 that doesn't need a frame buffer

causes.cause: The address jumpers on the back of the module (A0/A1/A2 solder pads) were changed
causes.check: Look at the solder pads on the back
causes.fix: Trust the scanner's address

entries.explain: Finding the address means the bus is working and the device is there, but the library is knocking on the wrong door number, so nobody answers. Just tell the library the number the scanner found.
entries.ask_ai: The I2C scanner found 0x[address]. I'm using a [module model] with the [library name] library and begin fails. Please tell me how to specify the address in this library, and whether allocation failed is a memory problem.

entries.symptom: The I2C device works with short wires, but once the wires are longer than about a foot (30cm) it gets flaky

causes.cause: I2C was designed for short on-board distances. Long wires add capacitance and blunt the signal edges
causes.check: Try 6-inch (15cm) wires
causes.fix: Shorten the wires; or Wire.setClock(100000) to drop to 100kHz; or use smaller pull-ups (2.2K)

causes.cause: The pull-up resistors are too large (10K) to drive long wires
causes.check: What pull-up value is on the module?
causes.fix: Add a 4.7K in parallel

causes.cause: The I2C wires are bundled with motor or power wires and picking up interference
causes.check: Route the I2C wires away from everything else
causes.fix: Separate them; use a twisted pair

entries.explain: An I2C signal is like pushing water through a soft hose: the longer the hose, the harder and slower each push. Dropping the speed gives each push more time; smaller pull-ups are like a stronger hand.
entries.ask_ai: An I2C [model] device on my STM32 is unreliable over [N] cm of wire. Please give me the STM32duino code to lower the I2C clock and a recommended pull-up resistor value.

entries.symptom: I2C works at first, then after some reset it stops responding completely; only a full power cycle brings it back
signals: only a power cycle fixes it

causes.cause: The reset happened in the middle of an I2C transfer, so the slave device is still waiting for the remaining clock pulses and holding SDA low
causes.check: Reproduce it: press RESET while a sensor read is in progress
causes.fix: In setup, before Wire.begin(), toggle SCL as a GPIO 9 times to release the bus; or simplest of all, cut power to the module whenever you reset

causes.cause: The slave device itself (some cheap sensors) locks up
causes.check: Only one particular module does this
causes.fix: Put a GPIO-controlled switch on that module's VCC so you can reboot it when it hangs

entries.explain: Two people are talking, and one of them loses their memory mid-sentence and restarts. The other is still waiting for the rest of the sentence, holding the line, never hanging up. Toggling SCL 9 times finishes the sentence on the other party's behalf.
entries.ask_ai: In STM32duino, my I2C bus locks up after a reset (SDA held low) and only recovers after a power cycle. Please give me setup code that recovers the I2C bus (the 9 SCL pulses technique).

entries.symptom: My SPI display (TFT) powers on to a white or fully lit screen and shows nothing

causes.cause: The pin definitions in the library don't match your actual wiring (CS, DC, and RST especially)
causes.check: Open the library config (TFT_eSPI's User_Setup.h, or the constructor in your code) and compare pin by pin
causes.fix: Line them up. The Blue Pill's hardware SPI1 is SCK=PA5, MISO=PA6, MOSI=PA7; CS/DC/RST can be any GPIO but must be set correctly

causes.cause: Wrong driver chip selected (ST7735 vs ST7789 vs ILI9341 all look alike)
causes.check: Check the seller's listing or the marking on the display's ribbon cable
causes.fix: Change the driver define in the library config

causes.cause: RST isn't connected or is on the wrong pin, so the display controller never got reset
causes.check: Wire RST to a GPIO and set that pin in the code
causes.fix: Connect it, or tie it to 3.3V (works on some displays)

causes.cause: SPI speed is too high (default 27MHz+) and fails once the wires get long
causes.check: Lower SPI_FREQUENCY to 8000000
causes.fix: Slow it down

entries.explain: A white screen is the display's factory idle state: the backlight is on, but the controller chip hasn't received a single command it understands. Either the commands are going to the wrong door (pins) or they're in a different dialect (driver chip).
entries.ask_ai: A [display model] SPI display on my STM32 Blue Pill shows a white screen. Wiring: SCK→[], MOSI→[], CS→[], DC→[], RST→[], BL→[]. The library is [library name]. Please give me the pin configuration code for this library and confirm the driver chip.

entries.symptom: The display lights up and shows something, but it's garbled, shifted, upside down, or the colors are inverted

causes.cause: Right driver chip, wrong variant (ST7735 comes in GREENTAB/REDTAB/BLACKTAB, each with a different offset)
causes.check: Try the different TAB variants in the library config
causes.fix: Try them one by one until nothing is shifted

causes.cause: Wrong resolution (128x160 entered as 128x128)
causes.check: Measure the screen and compare against the seller's listing
causes.fix: Fix the config

causes.cause: SPI speed too high, causing random speckles
causes.check: Drop to 8MHz
causes.fix: Slow it down; shorten the wires

causes.cause: Inverted colors: needs invertDisplay(true) or the RGB/BGR order setting
causes.check: If red shows up as blue, it's RGB/BGR
causes.fix: Change the color order in the config

entries.explain: Displays with the same driver chip from different manufacturers start counting "row one" from different spots in the pixel array. The library needs to know which offset yours uses, or the whole image lands shifted over.
entries.ask_ai: A [display model] on my STM32 shows an image but it's [garbled / shifted N pixels / upside down / inverted colors]. The library is [library name]. Please list every config option in this library that affects offset, rotation, or color order.

entries.symptom: The SD card module won't initialize; SD.begin() returns false

causes.cause: The CS pin wasn't passed to SD.begin(csPin)
causes.check: Does SD.begin have an argument?
causes.fix: SD.begin(PA4) or whichever pin matches your wiring

causes.cause: The card is formatted wrong (exFAT, or 64GB and up); the library only understands FAT16/FAT32
causes.check: Check the card's format on your computer
causes.fix: Use a card 32GB or smaller, formatted FAT32

causes.cause: The module is a 5V one (with a level shifter) but you gave it 3.3V
causes.check: Does the module have a 5V marking and a level-shifter chip?
causes.fix: Connect VCC to 5V

causes.cause: SPI initialization speed is too high
causes.check: SD.begin(cs, SPI_HALF_SPEED)
causes.fix: Slow it down

entries.explain: An SD card has to shake hands before it talks, and that handshake is picky about speed, format, and power. Most failures are a wrong card format or a CS pin the library was never told about.
entries.ask_ai: An SD card module on my STM32 Blue Pill fails SD.begin. CS is on [pin], the module is powered at [voltage], the card is [capacity] formatted as [format]. Please walk me through the causes in order of likelihood.

entries.symptom: My DHT11/DHT22 temperature and humidity sensor reads NaN or -999 or Failed to read
signals: Failed to read from DHT sensor

causes.cause: Reading too often. The DHT11 needs at least 1 second between reads, the DHT22 at least 2
causes.check: What's the delay in loop?
causes.fix: delay(2000)

causes.cause: Reading right after power-up, before the sensor is ready
causes.check: Is there a delay(2000) after dht.begin() in setup?
causes.fix: Add the delay

causes.cause: No pull-up on the data line (the bare 4-pin sensor needs a 10K pull-up; 3-pin modules usually have one built in)
causes.check: Is it a 3-pin module or a bare 4-pin part?
causes.fix: For the 4-pin version, add 10K between DATA and VCC

causes.cause: Wrong model: the code says DHT22 but it's actually a DHT11 (or the reverse)
causes.check: Case color: DHT11 is blue, DHT22 is white
causes.fix: Change #define DHTTYPE

causes.cause: Wires too long or loose
causes.check: Try shorter wires
causes.fix: Replace them

entries.explain: The DHT is a slow, deliberate sensor: after every measurement it needs a second or two of rest before it can measure again. Rush it and it hands you a NaN ("I don't know").
entries.ask_ai: A DHT[11/22] on my STM32 [pin] keeps reading NaN. It's a [3-pin module / bare 4-pin part], the library is [library name], and the loop delay is [N]ms. Please give me the correct read timing and wiring.

entries.symptom: My DS18B20 reads -127 or 85 degrees

causes.cause: -127 means no device found; the most common reason is a missing 4.7K pull-up (DATA to VCC)
causes.check: Is there a resistor between DATA and VCC?
causes.fix: Add a 4.7K pull-up. On the waterproof version's three wires: red VCC, black/yellow GND, yellow/white DATA (colors vary; go by the seller's description)

causes.cause: 85 means you read before the first conversion after power-up finished
causes.check: Only the very first reading is 85
causes.fix: After sensors.requestTemperatures(), delay(750) before getTempC

causes.cause: Wrong pin, or OneWire initialized on a different pin than the one you wired
causes.check: Compare OneWire oneWire(pin) in the code with the actual wiring
causes.fix: Fix it

causes.cause: Counterfeit chip (many cheap ones are) behaving strangely
causes.check: Try a different one
causes.fix: Replace it

entries.explain: The DS18B20 sends both power and data over one wire, and it relies on that pull-up resistor to hold the line high by default. Without it the line sits low and the chip thinks nobody's home. -127 is the library's code for "nobody answered"; 85 is the chip's code for "I haven't finished measuring yet."
entries.ask_ai: A DS18B20 on my STM32 [pin] reads [-127/85]. I [have / have not] added a 4.7K pull-up. The wire colors are [list]. Please give me the wiring and minimal code using the DallasTemperature library.

entries.symptom: My HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor reads 0 all the time or is all over the place, or I'm worried its 5V Echo will fry the board

causes.cause: The HC-SR04 needs 5V; on 3.3V it doesn't work or only reads very short distances
causes.check: Where is VCC connected?
causes.fix: Connect VCC to 5V

causes.cause: Echo outputs 5V and it's on a pin that isn't 5V-tolerant (especially PA0-PA7)
causes.check: Which pin is Echo on? Check for the FT tag in bluepill-pins.json
causes.fix: Move Echo to an FT pin (like PB5-PB15), or add a 1K + 2K voltage divider

causes.cause: pulseIn has no timeout, so it hangs for 1 second whenever there's no echo
causes.check: loop visibly stutters
causes.fix: pulseIn(echo, HIGH, 30000)

causes.cause: The Trig pulse is too short or wasn't pulled low first
causes.check: The standard sequence is LOW 2us → HIGH 10us → LOW
causes.fix: Follow the standard sequence

entries.explain: The ultrasonic module lives in the 5V world: it drinks 5V and it talks at 5V volume. The STM32 lives in the 3.3V world. To listen to 5V speech, it needs ears that can take it (FT pins) or a volume reducer (voltage divider).
entries.ask_ai: HC-SR04 on my STM32 Blue Pill. VCC→[], Trig→[], Echo→[]. Please confirm whether the Echo pin is 5V-tolerant, and give me distance-measuring code with a timeout.

entries.symptom: As soon as I connect a certain sensor module, the board reboots or gets hot, or the module never gives a reading

causes.cause: VCC and GND are reversed
causes.check: Cut power immediately. Recheck against the labels printed on the module
causes.fix: Rewire. Many modules die after a single reverse connection; if it doesn't work after rewiring, replace it

causes.cause: The module's VCC is on 5V but it only takes 3.3V (or the reverse)
causes.check: Find Operating Voltage on the module's product page or datasheet
causes.fix: Follow the datasheet

causes.cause: The module's pin order isn't what you assumed (GND-VCC-SDA-SCL and VCC-GND-SCL-SDA are both common)
causes.check: Don't wire by position; wire by the printed labels
causes.fix: Go by the labels

entries.explain: There's no industry standard for module pin order; the same kind of module from different makers can come in four or five different orders. Always read the labels, always wire with the power off, and always look one more time before powering up.
entries.ask_ai: After connecting a [module model] to my STM32, the board [reboots / gets hot / the module doesn't respond]. The module's pin labels from left to right are [list], and I wired them to [list]. Please check this.

entries.symptom: A motor wired straight to a GPIO pin won't spin, or spins briefly and stops, or that pin is dead afterward

causes.cause: A GPIO pin can only supply about 20mA; even a small motor draws hundreds of mA to start. Wired directly, it either won't spin or it fries the pin
causes.check: Is there a driver chip, MOSFET, or transistor in between?
causes.fix: Add a driver: for small DC motors use an L9110S/TB6612/L298N module, or an NPN transistor plus a diode. Give the motor its own power supply and tie grounds together

causes.cause: There is a driver, but its VCC or motor power isn't connected
causes.check: Is the power LED on the driver module lit?
causes.fix: The driver's motor power input (VM) needs a supply that can deliver the current

causes.cause: The pin is already fried
causes.check: Use that pin to light an LED. Does it work?
causes.fix: Switch pins. From now on, GPIO pins carry signals only, never loads

entries.explain: A GPIO pin is a fingertip: it can press buttons, but it can't carry a bucket of water. A motor is the bucket. You hire a weightlifter (the driver chip) to carry it, and your finger just tells the weightlifter what to do.
entries.ask_ai: I want to control a [voltage/model] DC motor with my STM32 Blue Pill, and I have [driver module model / no driver]. Please give me the wiring (including how power is routed and the common ground) and code for forward/reverse.

entries.symptom: The relay module's LED lights up, but I don't hear a click and nothing switches

causes.cause: The relay coil needs 5V but the module's VCC is on 3.3V, or the 3.3V GPIO can't drive the 5V module's optocoupler
causes.check: Try VCC on 5V; if that doesn't work, look for a JD-VCC jumper on the module
causes.fix: Connect VCC to 5V; if there's a JD-VCC jumper, remove the cap, put JD-VCC on 5V and VCC on 3.3V

causes.cause: The module is low-level trigger and you're writing HIGH to engage it
causes.check: Try writing LOW
causes.fix: Go by the module's label (Low Level Trigger) and invert your logic

causes.cause: USB can't supply enough power, and the board resets the moment the relay engages
causes.check: Does the serial output show setup running over and over?
causes.fix: Power the relay module from its own 5V supply

entries.explain: Inside a relay is an electromagnet that has to pull a metal contact over, and it needs a full 5V meal to do it. 3.3V is enough to light the indicator LED but leaves the electromagnet too weak to pull.
entries.ask_ai: A [N]-channel relay module on my STM32 Blue Pill won't engage. The module is labeled [high/low level trigger], VCC is on [voltage], IN is on [pin]. Please give me the wiring and test code.

entries.symptom: The instant a motor or servo starts, the board reboots, the serial output turns to garbage, or other sensors go haywire

causes.cause: The motor and the board share one power supply, and the motor's startup surge drags the voltage down
causes.check: Move the motor to its own supply (keep the common ground). Does it still reset?
causes.fix: Separate power plus common ground

causes.cause: Sparks and back-EMF from the motor wires are traveling back along the ground
causes.check: Is there a capacitor across the motor terminals?
causes.fix: Put a 0.1uF capacitor across the motor terminals; add a flyback diode for DC motors; add 100uF + 0.1uF at the power input

causes.cause: Signal wires are bundled together with the motor wires
causes.check: Route them separately
causes.fix: Separate them; keep signal wires short

entries.explain: A motor starting up is like someone on the same water line cranking a huge faucet wide open: your pressure drops to zero for an instant. Give the motor its own water line (separate supply) and only share the drain (GND).
entries.ask_ai: My STM32 board resets or its sensors glitch whenever a [motor/servo/relay] operates. Current power setup: [describe]. Please recommend a power topology (as a text diagram) and tell me which capacitors and diodes to add.

entries.symptom: The LED is very dim, or it flashed bright and died, or only the first LED on the strip lights up

causes.cause: A plain LED with no current-limiting resistor in series; too much current burned it out
causes.check: Is there a resistor between the LED and the pin?
causes.fix: Put a 220Ω-1K resistor in series

causes.cause: A WS2812 strip's data line wants 5V logic; 3.3V is borderline and whether it works is luck
causes.check: Only the first LED lights, or the colors are wrong
causes.fix: Add a 74HCT125 level shifter on the data line; or power just the first LED from 3.7V so it acts as the shifter

causes.cause: The strip is drawing power from the board's 5V pin; with many LEDs at full brightness that's several amps, which it can't supply
causes.check: Do only a few LEDs light, or all of them? Does white shift color?
causes.fix: Separate 5V supply; budget about 3A per meter

entries.explain: An LED has no self-control: it eats as much current as you give it, right up until it dies. The resistor is the portion-control spoon.
entries.ask_ai: I want to connect [a plain LED / a WS2812 strip with N LEDs] to my STM32. Please give me the specific plan for resistors, level shifting, and power, plus minimal code.

entries.symptom: Everything works until I connect one particular peripheral, then it all falls apart: reboots, dimming, serial dropping out

causes.cause: A computer's USB port only gives 500mA; after the board takes its share, there's very little left for peripherals
